statement: Of the various methods suggested for bleaching palm oil, the bichromate process originated by Watts is undoubtedly the best. In the bichromate process, one molecule of potassium bichromate reacts with fourteen of hydrochloric acid to give two of potassium chloride, one of chromic chloride, seven of water and six atoms of chlorine, and the six atoms of chlorine react with three molecules of water to give six of hydrochloric acid and three atoms of oxygen. In practice it is necessary to use twice the amount of acid required by theory.
source_passage: Of the various methods suggested for bleaching palm oil, the bichromate process originated by Watts is undoubtedly the best. The reaction may be expressed by the following equation, though in practice it is necessary to use twice the amount of acid required by theory:-- K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7} + 14HCl = 2KCl + Cr_{2}Cl_{6} + 7H_{2}O + 6Cl. 6Cl + 3H_{2}O = 6HCl + 3O.

statement: Before bleaching by the bichromate process, palm oil is freed from solid impurities by melting and subsidence, placed in the bleaching tank and washed with water containing a little hydrochloric acid; after resting, the liquor and sediment (chiefly sand) are drawn off. The bleaching reagent for palm oil consists of potassium bichromate and commercial muriatic acid: for every ton of oil, 22 to 28 lb. potassium bichromate and 45 to 60 lb. acid will be found sufficient to produce a good bleached oil.
source_passage: The palm oil, freed from solid impurities by melting and subsidence, is placed in the bleaching tank, and washed with water containing a little hydrochloric acid. Having allowed it to rest, and drawn off the liquor and sediment (chiefly sand), the palm oil is ready for treatment with the bleaching reagent, which consists of potassium bichromate and commercial muriatic acid. For every ton of oil, 22 to 28 lb. potassium bichromate and 45 to 60 lb. acid will be found sufficient to produce a good bleached oil.

statement: In bleaching palm oil by the bichromate process, the best procedure is to act on the colouring matter three successive times, using in the first two treatments one-third of the average of the quantities of bichromate and acid per ton, and in the final treatment a quantity gauged by the appearance of a cooled sample of the oil. The potassium bichromate is dissolved in hot water and added to the crude palm oil, previously heated to 125 deg. F. (52 deg. C.); the muriatic acid is then run in and the whole well agitated by means of air. The bright red colour of the palm oil gradually changes to dark brown and soon becomes green; after a few minutes agitation is stopped, the mixture is allowed to settle and the green liquor is withdrawn.
source_passage: The best procedure is to act upon the colouring matter of the oil three successive times, using in the first two treatments one-third of the average of the figures just given, and in the final treatment an appropriate quantity which can be easily gauged by the appearance of a cooled sample of the oil. The potassium bichromate is dissolved in hot water and added to the crude palm oil, previously heated to 125 deg. F. (52 deg. C.), the requisite amount of muriatic acid being then run in and the whole well agitated by means of air. The bright red colour of the oil gradually changes to dark brown, and soon becomes green. The action having proceeded for a few minutes, agitation is stopped, and, after allowing to settle, the green liquor is withdrawn.

statement: When sufficiently bleached by the bichromate process, palm oil is finally washed, without further heating, with hot water (which may contain salt) to remove the last traces of chrome liquor; if the operation is carried out carefully, the colouring matter will be completely oxidised. The temperature must not be allowed to rise above 130 deg. F. (54 deg. C.) during the bleaching of palm oil, otherwise the resultant oil on saponification is apt to yield a soap of a "foxy" colour. Bleached palm oil retains the characteristic violet odour of the original oil. Dilute sulphuric acid, or a mixture of dilute sulphuric acid and common salt, has been suggested in place of muriatic acid in the bichromate process.
source_passage: When sufficiently bleached the oil is finally washed (without further heating) with hot water (which may contain salt), to remove the last traces of chrome liquor. If the above operation is carried out carefully, the colouring matter will be completely oxidised. It is important, however, that the temperature should not be allowed to rise above 130 deg. F. (54 deg. C.) during the bleaching of palm oil, otherwise the resultant oil on saponification is apt to yield a soap of a "foxy" colour. The bleached oil retains the characteristic violet odour of the original oil. It has been suggested to use dilute sulphuric acid, or a mixture of this and common salt, in the place of muriatic acid in the above process.

statement: The deep colouring matter of crude cotton-seed oil, together with its mucilaginous and resinous principles, is removed by refining with caustic soda lye. The chief aim of the cotton-seed oil refiner is to remove these impurities without saponifying any of the neutral oil; the percentage of free fatty acids in the oil determines the quantity of caustic lye required, which must only be sufficient to remove this acidity.
source_passage: The deep colouring matter of crude cotton-seed oil, together with the mucilaginous and resinous principles, are removed by refining with caustic soda lye. The chief aim of the refiner is to remove these impurities without saponifying any of the neutral oil. The percentage of free fatty acids in the oil will determine the quantity of caustic lye required, which must only be sufficient to remove this acidity.

statement: In refining crude cotton-seed oil, the quantity of caustic soda lye needed to neutralise the free acidity is diluted with water to 12 deg. or 15 deg. Tw. (8 deg. or 10 deg. B.), and the refining is carried out in three stages. The oil is heated in a tank by a closed steam coil to 100 deg. F. (38 deg. C.), a third of the weak lye is added in a fine stream or by a sprinkler, and the whole is well agitated with a mechanical agitator or by blowing air through a pipe laid on the bottom of the tank. Prolonged agitation with air tends to oxidise cotton-seed oil, which increases its specific gravity and refractive index and produces a reddish soap in the soap-pan. As the treatment proceeds, the temperature may be carefully raised by the steam coil to 120 deg. F. (49 deg. C.).
source_passage: Having determined the amount of free acidity, the quantity of caustic soda lye necessary to neutralise it is diluted with water to 12 deg. or 15 deg. Tw. (8 deg. or 10 deg. B.), and the refining process carried out in three stages. The oil is placed in a suitable tank and heated by means of a closed steam coil to 100 deg. F. (38 deg. C.), a third of the necessary weak caustic soda lye added in a fine stream or by means of a sprinkler, and the whole well agitated with a mechanical agitator or by blowing a current of air through a pipe laid on the bottom of the tank. Prolonged agitation with air has a tendency to oxidise the oil, which increases its specific gravity and refractive index, and will be found in the soap-pan to produce a reddish soap. As the treatment proceeds, the temperature may be carefully raised, by means of the steam coil, to 120 deg. F. (49 deg. C.).

statement: In refining crude cotton-seed oil, after the first treatment has proceeded fifteen minutes the contents of the tank are allowed to rest, the settling being prolonged as much as possible, say overnight, so that the impurities precipitate well and carry down the least amount of entangled oil. The coloured "foots" are withdrawn, the second portion of weak caustic soda solution is agitated with the partially refined oil, and after resting the settled coloured liquor is drawn off. The final treatment is performed in the same manner as the two previous ones, and on settling a clear yellow oil separates.
source_passage: The first treatment having proceeded fifteen minutes, the contents of the tank are allowed to rest; the settling should be prolonged as much as possible, say overnight, to allow the impurities to precipitate well, and carry down the least amount of entangled oil. Having withdrawn these coloured "foots," the second portion of the weak caustic soda solution is agitated with the partially refined oil, and, when the latter is sufficiently treated, it is allowed to rest and the settled coloured liquor drawn off as before. The oil is now ready for the final treatment, which is performed in the same manner as the two previous ones. On settling, a clear yellow oil separates.

statement: After refining, cotton-seed oil may be brightened and filtered to produce a marketable article, but this may be omitted if the oil is refined for own use in the soap-house. The residue or "foots" from refining crude cotton-seed oil, known in the trade as "mucilage", may be converted into "soapstock", or decomposed by a mineral acid and made into "black grease" ready for distillation by superheated steam.
source_passage: If desired, the oil may be brightened and filtered, after refining to produce a marketable article, but if it is being refined for own use in the soap-house, this may be omitted. The residue or "foots" produced during the refining of crude cotton-seed oil, known in the trade as "mucilage," may be converted into "soapstock" as mentioned in the preceding chapter, or decomposed by a mineral acid and made into "black grease" ready for distillation by superheated steam.

statement: The other vegetable oils used in soap-making come to the soap-maker in a refined condition, but occasionally it is desirable to remove a portion of their free fatty acids, a treatment that also causes the colouring matter to be precipitated. The treatment brings the oil and a weak solution of caustic lye into intimate contact, and cocoa-nut oil is often treated in this manner. Sometimes it is only necessary to agitate the oil well with 1-1/2 per cent. of its weight of a 12 deg. Tw. (8 deg. B.) solution of caustic soda and allow it to settle. The foots from this treatment of vegetable oils are utilised in the soap-pan.
source_passage: The other vegetable oils come to the soap-maker's hand in a refined condition; occasionally, however, it is desirable to remove a portion of the free fatty acids, which treatment also causes the colouring matter to be preciptated. This is effected by bringing the oil and a weak solution of caustic lye into intimate contact. Cocoa-nut oil is often treated in this manner. Sometimes it is only necessary to well agitate the oil with 1-1/2 per cent. of its weight of a 12 deg. Tw. (8 deg. B.) solution of caustic soda and allow to settle. The foots are utilised in the soap-pan.

statement: Tallows are often greatly improved by the alkaline treatment with weak caustic soda at 165 deg. F. (73 deg. C.). The alkaline treatment of tallow is one of the best methods and has advantages over acid processes: the caustic soda removes the free acid and bodies of aldehyde nature (most probably the result of oxidation or polymerisation) while the neutral fat is not attacked, and the alkaline foots can be used in the production of soap.
source_passage: Tallows are often greatly improved by the above alkaline treatment at 165 deg. F. (73 deg. C.). It is one of the best methods and possesses advantages over acid processes--the caustic soda removes the free acid and bodies of aldehyde nature, which are most probably the result of oxidation or polymerisation, whereas the neutral fat is not attacked, and further, the alkaline foots can be used in the production of soap.

statement: Bone fat often contains calcium (lime) salts, which are very objectionable substances in a soap-pan and must be removed by treatment with hydrochloric or sulphuric acid. Hydrochloric acid is preferable for bone fat, as the lime salt formed is readily soluble and easily removed. The bone fat is agitated with a weak solution of acid in a lead-lined tank by blowing in steam; when the treatment is complete and the waste liquor withdrawn, the last traces of acid are well washed out of the liquid fat with hot water.
source_passage: Bone fat often contains calcium (lime) salts, which are very objectionable substances in a soap-pan. These impurities must be removed by a treatment with hydrochloric or sulphuric acid. The former acid is preferable, as the lime salt formed is readily soluble and easily removed. The fat is agitated with a weak solution of acid in a lead-lined tank by blowing in steam, and when the treatment is complete and the waste liquor withdrawn, the last traces of acid are well washed out of the liquid fat with hot water.

statement: Several methods have been suggested for bleaching rosin; some alter the constitution of the rosin, and in others the cost is too great or the process impracticable. The aim of rosin bleaching must be to eliminate the colouring matter without altering the original properties of the rosin, and this is best carried out by converting the rosin into resinate of soda by boiling it with a solution of either caustic soda or carbonated alkali.
source_passage: Several methods have been suggested for bleaching rosin; in some instances the constitution of the rosin is altered, and in others the cost is too great or the process impracticable. The aim of these processes must necessarily be the elimination of the colouring matter without altering the original properties of the substance. This is best carried out by converting the rosin into a resinate of soda by boiling it with a solution of either caustic soda or carbonated alkali.

statement: In bleaching rosin with caustic soda, 37 cwt. of 17 deg. Tw. (11 deg. B.) caustic soda lye is heated, 20 cwt. of rosin broken into pieces is added, and the boiling is continued until all the resinate is homogeneous; 1-1/2 cwt. of salt is then added and the boiling prolonged a little. On resting, the coloured liquor rises to the surface of the resinate and may be siphoned off (or pumped away through a skimmer pipe), and the resinate is further washed with water containing a little salt.
source_passage: The process is commenced by heating 37 cwt. of 17 deg. Tw. (11 deg. B.) caustic soda lye, and adding 20 cwt. of rosin, broken into pieces, and continuing the boiling until all the resinate is homogeneous, when an addition of 1-1/2 cwt. of salt is made and the boiling prolonged a little. On resting, the coloured liquor rises to the surface of the resinate, and may be siphoned off (or pumped away through a skimmer pipe) and the resinate further washed with water containing a little salt.

statement: In bleaching rosin with carbonated alkali, a solution of 2-3/4 cwt. of soda ash (58 deg.) in about four times its weight of water is heated, 20 cwt. of rosin broken into small pieces is added, and the whole is heated by the open steam coil, and care must be taken to avoid boiling over; owing to the liberation of CO2 gas, frothing takes place. Many patents have been granted for the preparation of resinate of soda, with methods devised to obviate the boiling over: some mix the rosin and soda ash (or only a portion of the soda ash) before dissolving in water; others saponify in a boiler connected with a trap which returns the resinate to the pan and allows the carbonic-acid gas to escape or to be collected.
source_passage: The treatment with carbonated alkali is performed in a similar manner. A solution, consisting of 2-3/4 cwt. of soda ash (58 deg.), in about four times its weight of water, is heated and 20 cwt. of rosin, broken into small pieces, added. The whole is heated by means of the open steam coil, and care must be taken to avoid boiling over. Owing to the liberation of CO_{2} gas, frothing takes place. A large number of patents have been granted for the preparation of resinate of soda, and many methods devised to obviate the boiling over. Some suggest mixing the rosin and soda ash (or only a portion of the soda ash) prior to dissolving in water; others saponify in a boiler connected with a trap which returns the resinate to the pan and allows the carbonic-acid gas to escape or to be collected.

statement: With due precaution, the carbonated alkali method of making resinate of soda can easily be worked in open vessels, and with the proportions given (2-3/4 cwt. of soda ash to 20 cwt. of rosin) enough uncombined rosin remains for the product to be pumped into the soap with which it is to be mixed, where it is finally saponified thoroughly. The salt required in making resinate of soda, 1-1/2 cwt. in the example given, may be added to the solution before the rosin or sprinkled in towards the finish of the boiling. When the whole has been sufficiently boiled and allowed to rest, the liquor containing the colouring matter floats over the resinate and, after removal, may be replaced by another washing.
source_passage: With due precaution the method can be easily worked in open vessels, and, using the above proportions, there will be sufficient uncombined rosin remaining to allow the resultant product to be pumped into the soap with which it is intended to intermix it, where it will be finally saponified thoroughly. The salt required, which, in the example given, would be 1-1/2 cwt., may be added to the solution prior to the addition of rosin or sprinkled in towards the finish of the boiling. When the whole has been sufficiently boiled and allowed to rest, the liquor containing the colouring matter will float over the resinate, and, after removal, may be replaced by another washing.

statement: Many other methods have been suggested for bleaching, refining and treating materials intended for saponification, but the practical processes described for palm oil, cotton-seed oil, other vegetable oils, tallow, bone fat and rosin are successfully employed. All fats and oils, after being melted by the aid of steam, must be allowed to settle thoroughly, and the condensed water and impurities withdrawn through a trap arrangement for collecting the fatty matter. Molten, settled fatty materials on their way to the soap-pan should be passed through sieves fine enough to free them from suspended matter.
source_passage: Many other methods have been suggested for the bleaching, refining and treatment of materials intended for saponification, but the above practical processes are successfully employed. All fats and oils after being melted by the aid of steam must be allowed to thoroughly settle, and the condensed water and impurities withdrawn through a trap arrangement for collecting the fatty matter. The molten settled fatty materials _en route_ to the soap-pan should be passed through sieves sufficiently fine to free them from suspended matter.
